extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy writers / comedians (especially those writing topical one-liners or monologue jokes)
extracted.subtask_description: Turning a topical news item into a short, laugh-producing joke (one-liner/monologue line), using idea selection, associative linking, drafting, and focused rewriting for clarity, believability, and platform constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic selection via emotional reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have an emotional reaction to the headline—'That’s weird'—which alerts me that the news item might be of general interest and worth exploring as a joke Topic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick topics that provoke an immediate emotional response (weird, shocking, relatable). That response indicates potential interest and comedic value. Example: the 'Giant African Snails Seized at Los Angeles Airport' headline triggered 'that's weird' and became a usable Topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose Topics with multiple 'handles' (associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The news item also feels promising because it has two handles–'snail' and 'Los Angeles'—each of which has several well-known associations. That means there’s a great chance I can create a solid Punch Line from the associations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer topics that contain multiple recognizable elements (nouns/places/etc.) you can map to associations. More 'handles' increases the chance of finding a strong link for a punch line. Example associations: 'snail' → slimy, slow, eaten by French; 'Los Angeles' → smog, traffic, celebrities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate Punch Lines by focusing on strong, well-known associations
rubrics_metrics.description: "To generate a Punch Line, I focus first on the well-known 'snail' association 'slow' and ask myself which slow people are commonly associated with Los Angeles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a dominant, easily recognized association for your Topic and find another target that shares that association; the unexpected comparison yields the joke. Example: link 'slow' (snail) to 'slow workers' (DMV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research/tools to spark idea generation
rubrics_metrics.description: "To spark ideas I Google 'slow workers,' which reminds me of the DMV."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When associations don't come immediately, use simple searches or brainstorming tools to surface culturally-shared targets or tropes to connect to your Topic. This helps locate an effective Punch Line target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a shared association to link Topic and Punch Line
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in the method: link the Topic and Punch Line by a shared association (e.g., both are 'slow').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly articulate the shared trait or association that will form the connective logic of the joke—this is the conceptual bridge that makes the comparison feel coherent and surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a rough draft linking Topic → Punch Line
rubrics_metrics.description: "Partial Rough Draft: 'Giant African snails were seized at Los Angeles Airport…workers at the DMV.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get an initial sentence or two down that establishes the Topic and delivers the Punch Line, even if clumsy. Rough drafts let you see the connection and identify what needs smoothing (angle, clarity, plausibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Add an Angle to explain the connection smoothly and efficiently
rubrics_metrics.description: "To complete my rough draft I need an Angle that connects my Topic and Punch Line smoothly and efficiently."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Angle provides the causal or explanatory step that makes the punchline believable and understandable in few words. Example: explain how snails became DMV employees: 'Instead of destroying them, officials gave them jobs at the DMV.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generic authority words to avoid distracting specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: "I use the word 'officials' a lot in topical jokes. It suggests authority figures but isn’t specific enough to be distracting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming actors, prefer broad, non-distracting terms (officials, authorities) unless a specific actor adds value. Over-specificity can pull focus from the joke's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify plausibility by specifying animate/functional details
rubrics_metrics.description: "I add 'live shipment' to clarify that these creatures are animate and could conceivably perform some kind of work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief clarifying details that make the absurd premise seem possible enough to accept. Small clarifications (e.g., 'live shipment') help the audience imagine the comedic scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small factual details to reinforce believability
rubrics_metrics.description: "I add '67' because that detail from the news story subtly reinforces that this incident actually occurred."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including a concrete detail (numbers, locations) can make a topical joke feel grounded and credible, increasing the payoff. Use such details judiciously; they should support, not distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove unnecessary or distracting specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: "I remove 'African' because it’s distractingly specific and unnecessary for the joke."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim details that don't contribute to the joke's logic or that introduce irrelevant associations. Extraneous specificity can dilute the focus or create unwanted implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat the key noun for emphasis and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "I repeat 'snails' in the Angle because it’s so crucial to making the Punch Line work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition of the central word/concept in setup and angle helps maintain focus and strengthens the link to the punchline. Use strategic repetition rather than redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backload the Topic: move important elements closer to the Punch Line
rubrics_metrics.description: "I backload the Topic, moving the most important elements closer to the Punch Line."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange sentence elements so the setup puts crucial information nearer to the ending/punch. This tightens momentum and increases impact. Example: restructure sentences to bring the subject into position before the punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active voice and specific actors for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "I add 'customs inspectors' to get rid of the passive voice and to clarify why the snails were seized and might be destroyed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using active constructions and naming plausible actors clarifies causality and makes the scenario crisper. Replace passive phrasing with an agent when it aids understanding and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit for platform length constraints without weakening the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: "Abbreviating the name of the airport took the joke down to exactly 140 characters, Twitter’s limit at the time. That meant I didn’t have to waste more time, and possibly weaken the joke, trimming it to fit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you must fit a platform limit (e.g., Twitter), prefer concise edits (abbreviations, tightening phrasing) that preserve the joke’s logic and punch rather than reworking core elements and risking loss of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy Quality Tests: check for hackiness and freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the tests gives me pause: Is the joke too familiar? Is making fun of slow DMV employees similar to making fun of airline food–too hacky? I decide that the joke is so effective that the laugh will blow away any possible whiff of hackiness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before posting, evaluate whether the premise or target is cliché or overused. If it’s familiar, judge whether the specific twist/punch is strong enough to overcome hackiness. If not, revise or discard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow an iterative process: idea → rough draft → rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: "Writing a joke is first thinking of what to write, then slapping together a rough draft, and only then rewriting to maximize the laugh."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat joke-writing as iterative: spend time on idea generation, produce a quick rough draft to test the concept, then rewrite for clarity, pacing, word choice, and maximum laugh. Rewriting is where the joke is sharpened.
